newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ATHLETICS-GREENE VYING FOR LEWIS'S MANTLE.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-GREENE VYING FOR LEWIS'S MANTLE.

text.p: The United States may at last have found a sprinter who has a chance of stepping into the shoes of Carl Lewis.

The 22-year-old Maurice Greene disposed of one of the fastest 100 metres fields ever assembled at the Lausanne grand prix on Wednesday, beating Canada's Olympic and world champion Donovan Bailey in the process.

While American champion Greene is certainly not capable of matching Lewis's remarkable record of Olympic golds in sprinting and long jumping, he is a hot tip to secure for the U.S. their first 100 metres title at a global event since 1991 at next month's world championships in Athens.
Talk to Greene for a few minutes and there are one or two flashes of Lewis's character which are immediately apparent.

He has a similar tone of voice and his sentences are dripping with confidence. Lewis-like soundbites are already flowing off his tongue and being lapped up by an American media hungry for another sprint champion who can raise the low profile of track and field in the country.
Most of all, Greene seems to have a sparkle in his eyes which Lewis had in his heyday. It indicates a belief that he can take the first 100 gold since Lewis won the world title in Tokyo in 1991.

Greene may choke on the big day, of course, and be ranked with the other American sprinters who have produced world-class performances in recent years but failed to win the important major 100 title -- like former world record holder Leroy Burrell and ex-Olympic bronze medallist Dennis Mitchell.
But Wednesday's victory in the rain in an impressive 9.90 seconds told another story.
"I am very positive about Athens. I want to bring U.S. sprinting back to where it is supposed to be. It has not gone. It just needs someone to step up and take charge," Greene said.
"I am learning every day and there is a lot more to learn. There is only pressure when you think you can't do something...There is no pressure on me. I am just trying to have fun."

The Lausanne field was one of the fastest ever assembled outside an Olympic or world championship final. Six of the eight sprinters had run under 10 seconds already this season. The race included six of the finalists at last year's Olympics and all three medallists -- Bailey, Namibia's Frankie Fredericks and Ato Boldon of Trinidad.

Greene was pushed all the way, Fredericks taking second only one hundreth of a second behind in 9.91 with Bailey third in 9.97. Britain's Linford Christie, who took over Lewis's 100 crown at the 1992 Barcelona Olympics and 1993 world championships, could finish only seventh in 10.12. Boldon was sixth in 10.08.

Greene failed to make an impact at his first world championships in the Swedish city of Gothenburg in 1995. But although Bailey tried to talk down the Lausanne defeat, the Canadian and his rivals know they will have to take the American seriously in Athens.

"If I'm on their minds, then that is good for me. I am not a star," Greene said. "I haven't accomplished the goals I have yet. After Athens I could be a star after I have done something good. Good for me means first place. I don't run to get second or third. You shouldn't be running if you think like that."
"I didn't run well in Gothenburg. There was a lot on my mind. It was my first time...I put pressure on myself...(Now) I can handle the pressure."

Bailey must now work on getting back the kind of devastating final burst which swept the towering sprinter to the 100 crown in a world record 9.84 seconds at last year's Atlanta Olympics. He described his last half of the race in Lausanne as "pathetic at best."

Bailey was also beaten by Fredericks in a similar high- class race in Lausanne last season but bounced back in Atlanta. But Greene is likely to mount a serious challenge to the Canadian this time, however.
